missionPremise: Sylvia Carrillo (Bastrop city manager) asked to model what happens when four inches of rain falls on a property, to screen out sites that plainly do not need a drainage engineer. The dispatch's framing ('the engine already answers her question; nobody has ever been able to ask it') was directionally right but imprecise: verification showed the engine route, engine-api, AND hauska-map's own BFF (pe-flood-drainage-core.ts) already fully validated and forwarded rainfallDepthInches end to end before this row started. The actual, narrower gap: the PE client function requestFloodDrainageRefresh(parcelNodeId) took no depth argument at all, and no UI control existed. This is reported as a refinement of the dispatch's own premise, per its instruction to verify before building rather than accept the framing as given.

cacheMissAndTimeoutDetermination: NOT a cache miss in any sense that differentiates custom depth from default: flood-drainage-study.ts has no refresh-level caching at any depth -- every POST /refresh call (default or custom) re-fetches the DEM and re-runs pysheds from scratch; the only 'cached' path is the separate GET /study read, orthogonal to which depth produced the cached payload. The dispatch's cited 85-154s timeout risk is real but belongs to a DIFFERENT report (feasibility, pe-feasibility-export-handler.ts, its own FEASIBILITY_ENGINE_TIMEOUT_MS) with its own already-in-flight, separately-scoped fix (P-155 / mission_p155_feasibility_async.md, currently reopened per F23). Live timing across 3 real calls on 2 fresh revisions showed the FIRST call to a cold container took 92.5-102.8s regardless of depth, while a SECOND call to an already-warm container took 12.0s -- container/subprocess cold-start (hydrologyWorkerClient.ts spawns a fresh python3 process per request), not the rainfall depth, is the dominant latency driver. Decision: reused the existing synchronous refresh + existing timeout/retry handling (FLOOD_ENGINE_TIMEOUT_MS, the retryable engine_timeout/unreachable 503 shape already wired into the client) rather than building new async-refresh/polling infrastructure -- the control introduces no differential timeout risk over the feature's pre-existing default-depth risk profile, and duplicating P-155's in-flight infrastructure for an unrelated report would be real scope creep.
